stories.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company
stories.summary: The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NU6L Milrem Robotics makes autonomous unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine [FILE: December 2022] Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement NATO and EU leaders rallied behind Estonia on Tuesday, after the Baltic country accused Russia of being behind an arson attack in its capital Tallinn. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Moscow was found responsible for the August 15 arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics, after the government conducted an investigation into the incident. Milrem Robotics develops ground drones that are used in Ukraine . "We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Tsahkna said on X, adding that the perpetrators had been arrested, and Russia's ambassador had been summoned. "This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe , aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna said. NATO chief Mark Rutte backed Estonia, accusing Russia of furthering "its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies."

stories.article_text_excerpt: The number of schools in Russia has fallen by 45% since the start of the century, with rural communities losing the most, according to a report by the Higher School of Economics published this month.Russia's secondary school network has shrunk from 68,800 institutions in 2000 to just under 38,000 in 2026, the report says. The school-age population has fallen by around 13.5% over the same period, from 20.5 million to 17.7 million children.Russia now has fewer schools than Germany, even though its population is roughly half the size. Germany has more than 40,000 schools in 2026.Closures have been most severe in rural areas, where the number of state schools has fallen from more than 45,000 to around 21,000, a reduction of more than half.Urban schools have also declined, from 22,700 in 2000 to 16,300 today. The number of pupils each school serves has grown substantially over the same period: from around 300 pupils per school 15 years ago to around 470 today.Private schools have increased in number, from 635 in 2000 to 982 in 2026, but account for only 2.5% of total provision.Is bigger always better?The closures stem from an optimisation programme launched in 2001 that remains ongoing.
